intro: Three readings were assigned with the course materials: one skeptic's case against the conspiracy theories, and two on method. Summaries are ours; read the originals for the arguments in full.

readings.title: The JFK Assassination: Conspiracy Theories at 50
readings.author: Dave Reitzes
readings.summary: A skeptic's review, written for the 50th anniversary, of why conspiracy belief took hold and why the author thinks the evidence still points to Oswald alone.
points: Origins. Ruby's killing of Oswald, the credibility gap of the Johnson years, Vietnam and Watergate made a conspiracy feel right; Jefferson Morley calls the case a national Rorschach test of attitudes toward government.
Earwitnesses. Of the dozens who described the shots' sound, very few said they came from more than one direction, but those few became the critics' star witnesses.

Parkland doctors. Their first impressions of a frontal entry are explained as the product of emergency conditions; they never turned the President over, and the autopsy photos and X-rays show entry from behind.

Photographic "gunmen." Figures on the knoll in the Moorman photo (including David Lifton's early find) and the "Umbrella Man" proved to be artifacts or innocent: Louie Steven Witt testified in 1978 that his umbrella was a political protest.
Mysterious deaths. Lists of supposedly suspicious deaths are mostly people who weren't witnesses, and few of the deaths were mysterious; no actuarial basis supports the claim.

Head snap. Forensic pathologists (Vincent Di Maio; even Cyril Wecht in another case) reject the idea that a bullet must push the head in its own direction; the backward movement is attributed to a neuromuscular reaction.

Disinformation and predisposition. Soviet outlets blamed a right-wing cabal within hours, and the KGB later forged documents tying Oswald to the CIA; some early critics were suspicious before seeing any evidence.
The CIA and Dulles. Johnson appointed Allen Dulles to the Warren Commission at Robert Kennedy's request, and the Kennedys continued to praise him after the Bay of Pigs.
Vietnam. Reports that Kennedy planned to withdraw are recollections that may be colored by later politics; the announced 1,000-man reduction was small.
Ruby. People who knew him called him a talker who couldn't keep a secret and an emotional man with a temper, the opposite of a mob hit man.

The physical case. Three shells and the Carcano on the sixth floor; ballistics match the shells, the nearly whole bullet and the large fragments to that rifle to the exclusion of all others; Oswald bought it by mail under an alias, and his palm print was on it.
Single bullet. Not invented to fit the Zapruder timing: pathologist James Humes first raised it after finding the neck bullet struck no bone.
Motive. A radical, unstable Castro admirer who had already shot at General Walker kills the man Castro called his enemy at a time when U.S. covert action against Castro was real.
Why it matters. Drawing on David Aaronovitch and research on conspiracy thinking, conspiracism correlates with rejecting science, with harmful results (for example on vaccines).
readings.evidence: Many items in both matrices cite it, usually as the counterweight to the advocacy chronologies.

readings.title: Evidence as a Multi-Disciplinary Subject
readings.author: William Twining
readings.summary: A legal theorist argues that evidence should be studied across disciplines (law, forensic science, intelligence analysis, medicine, history) and that what unifies it is inferential reasoning.
points: Evidence is a subject in its own right, not just the rules of admissibility; the "law of evidence" is a small, exclusionary part of reasoning about facts.
Following David Schum, he favors a "substance-blind" approach: the logic of inference is the same whatever the field.

Post-9/11 reviews of U.S. intelligence used the language of evidence scholars: the danger of hypothesis-driven inquiry, the difference between building a hypothesis and testing it, too much information versus absence of evidence, ambiguity versus incompleteness, the value of alternative readings, mirror-imaging, and confusing the unfamiliar with the improbable.

In the Wigmorean tradition, arguments run from evidence to conclusion through background generalizations ("common sense"), and those generalizations are the weak link: our stock of knowledge is a soup of fact, myth, stereotype and speculation, not tested propositions.
Detectives, historians and intelligence analysts, unlike judges deciding a decided case, must both construct and test hypotheses, which calls for abduction and imagination.
Contested trials and causes célèbres such as Sacco and Vanzetti are where inference is hardest, because the facts themselves are in dispute.
readings.evidence: Why this site uses ACH: it separates generating hypotheses from testing them and makes the generalizations behind each rating visible.

readings.title: The Study of Politics: Logic, Approaches and Methods
readings.author: Nkwachukwu Orji
readings.pub: In E. Nweke and N. Orji (eds.), A Handbook of Political Science (Ebonyi State University, 2009), ch. 2
readings.summary: An introductory overview of how political scientists justify knowledge (logic), choose what to study (approaches) and gather and analyze data (methods).
points: Logic: research paradigms (positivist, modeled on the natural sciences and aiming at testable causal claims; interpretivist, aiming at the meanings actors give their world) and research strategies: inductive (observe first, then generalize, seeking confirmation) and deductive (after Popper: state a hypothesis, derive what should follow, and try to falsify it; a theory that survives is only corroborated).
Positivism, from Comte, looks for correlations and causes but warns that correlation alone does not prove causation.
Approaches: normative, institutional (old and "new" institutionalism, formal and informal rules of the game), behavioral, rational choice, and others such as Marxist, feminist and constructivist.
Methods of inquiry: experiment is rare in politics, so most work is observational: case studies, comparative analysis and statistical analysis.
Case studies can create and test theories, identify and test antecedent conditions and explain important events, but critics say they can't control for intervening variables or generalize well.
Data come from interviews, questionnaires, observation and documents, analyzed qualitatively or quantitatively.
readings.evidence: The assassination is a single, contested case: a case study whose evidence is mostly documents and testimony, which is why source credibility is rated for every item here.
